fix.summary: Change the statement that touches thousands of rows of support_tickets into a loop over at most 1,000 rows at a time, each its own statement, so none takes enough locks to escalate. An UPDATE loop's filter must leave out the rows it already changed, or it never ends. Inside one transaction the loop still holds every row it changed until the commit, but other sessions then wait only for those rows, not for the whole table. To learn which statement it is, start the event session below (culprit_lock_escalation): it keeps each escalation with its statement, in memory, at almost no cost.

findings.summary: SQL Server replaced the row and page locks on support_tickets with one lock on the whole table 5 times since it started, on Oct 11 at 11:06 UTC. It keeps no time for each, and Culprit has no earlier scan to compare with, so they may be old: the next scan compares with this one and says whether any happened since. An escalation happens when one statement takes about 5,000 locks on one index: SQL Server swaps them for a single lock on the whole table, and every other session that writes to support_tickets, or reads it without row versioning, waits until that statement's transaction ends. SQL Server doesn't record which statement it was, and none of the statements in the query history writes to it: look at jobs, migrations and maintenance that change many rows at once.
